cards.title: Free cash flow vs net income: inventory and tax timing as cash drivers
cards.summary: Read the cash flow statement to see why free cash flow diverges from net income, driven mainly by inventory build/sell-through and tax payment timing.
cards.use_when: Monthly or quarterly cash review for your store, especially when net income looks positive but your bank balance is falling, or you are deciding how much inventory to buy for the next selling season.
steps: Pull the cash flow statement alongside the income statement, not instead of it. Attribution: ecommerce finance commentary treats the cash flow statement as the operational view of the business.

Compare the change in inventory line to net income. If inventory rose (e.g., 335 to 448 in the source example), that is a cash outflow even though it may sit as an asset; if inventory fell because you sold through it, that is a cash inflow.

Check tax payments as a separate line. In the source example, months with tax payments showed cash out, and months with no payment effectively conserved cash — the payment timing, not the underlying tax liability, moved the number.

List the other large lumpy items (e.g., paying a software engineering team 100k in one month) and note them so you understand which month you 'lost' cash because of investment rather than trading losses.

Reconcile: explain the gap between net income and free cash flow by naming the specific drivers (large inventory purchase plus engineering payments; or sell-through of inventory plus no tax payment plus little engineering spend).

Use free cash flow as the operational view and net cash flow (after financing) as the holistic view: it answers whether the business can pay its debts and run itself at the same time. In the source example net cash flow was slightly lower than free cash flow because of leverage.

Warning sign from the source: ecommerce businesses often go broke not because they lose money per customer, but because they run out of liquidity from bad working capital dynamics — so treat the cash statement as the survival document, not the income statement.
caveats: The specific figures (335 to 448 inventory, 77k net income vs -95k free cash flow, 140 vs 272) are one case-study example, not benchmarks.
Net cash flow after financing is less operational because whether you have a loan is somewhat unrelated to how the business itself operates.

cards.title: Calculate contribution margin per order and post-marketing contribution
cards.summary: Structure an ecommerce P&L into net revenue, product COGS, gross margin, fulfillment, contribution margin, CAC and post-marketing contribution so each expense can be optimized separately.
cards.use_when: Setting or reviewing product-level and order-level profitability, or diagnosing why a store that looks profitable at gross margin is not producing operating income.
steps: Start at gross revenue (product sales plus tax collected where applicable) and subtract discounts and returns, then add shipping income you charge customers. Result: net revenue, which is effectively your AOV after discounts and returns for the period.

Split COGS into product cost (manufacturing plus import freight plus duties/taxes to get product to the warehouse) and keep it separate from fulfillment cost (pick and pack, packing materials, 3PL charges, shipping to customer). A generic P&L lumps these together; splitting them is what lets you see which line is moving.
Compute gross margin = net revenue minus product COGS. In the source case study it ran about 70–75%.
Compute contribution margin = net revenue minus product COGS minus fulfillment. In the source example, $134 net revenue with $64 contribution margin, just under 50%.

Compute CAC as total marketing spend divided by first-time purchases, then post-marketing contribution = contribution margin minus CAC. Source example: $22 and $12 post-marketing contribution per order, i.e. profitable on the first order at roughly a 1.5 contribution-margin-to-CAC ratio.
Check merchant/credit card processing fees and include them — the source uses about 2.75% of revenue as a working assumption.

Finally subtract operating expense per order to reach operating income. In the source example opex was about $8 and $6 per order and operating income was 11% and 5%, i.e. about $15 and $6 profit per unit.

Remember the leverage: small per-order changes (knocking a couple of dollars out of one line) multiplied across thousands of orders is the difference between tens of thousands of losses and tens of thousands of profit.
caveats: Gross margin is the highest figure, contribution margin lower, post-marketing contribution lowest — mixing the terms (calling gross margin contribution margin) causes wrong decisions.
All percentages in the source are one case-study supplement brand in a specific period; do not treat them as targets.

After the first order, returning customers generally carry little or no marketing cost, so first-order profitability is the ideal state — the source calls businesses with strong first-order profit exceptional.

cards.title: Treat discount and CAC as one acquisition cost pool
cards.summary: Discounts and marketing spend are mathematically equivalent per-customer costs, so combine them into a single budget and optimize the split for total profit, not per-customer margin.
cards.use_when: Planning next quarter's promotional calendar and ad budget, or deciding whether a deeper discount or more ad spend will grow profit for the whole store.
steps: Build the scenario grid with the same ad spend in every column, then vary the discount. Source case: $100,000 spend, $1.50 per click blended, ~66,667 sessions in all scenarios, undiscounted price $200, COGS $75 ($50 product + $25 fulfillment).

Convert discount into a conversion-rate assumption. Source assumptions: 0% discount → 1.5% website conversion → 1,000 purchases → $100 CAC; $30 discount → 2.2% → 1,433 purchases → $70 CAC; $60 discount → 3.8% → 2,500 purchases → $40 CAC.

Compute contribution margin post-CAC per customer for each scenario. In the source, all three land at $25 per customer, because discount plus CAC totals $100 in every scenario: 0% + $100, $30 + $70, $60 + $40.

Now total it up across the whole business. Source results: scenario A $200,000 sales, $125,000 pre-marketing contribution, $25,000 post-marketing; scenario B $243,000, $136,000, $36,000; scenario C $350,000, $162,000, $63,000. The deepest-discount scenario produced the most total profit in this particular case.
Do not assume the deepest discount always wins. The source states it can go both ways: some brands make more money by shrinking revenue with spectacular unit economics on a smaller base of customers.

Reframe your planning as one pool: 'we will spend $X this year on demand creation — how do we split it between discounts and ad platforms to maximize sales and profit?' Treat the discount line and the marketing line as two forms of the same cost of acquisition.

Prefer attaching your best discounts to a loyalty or subscription on-ramp rather than a flash sale. The source argues flash-sale converters often will not buy without a big discount, while customers who join a loyalty or subscription program have self-selected into higher lifetime value.
Run this as a future-strategy split test with identical spend before committing to the deeper discount calendar.
caveats: The 1.5%/2.2%/3.8% conversion lifts and the $1.50 CPC are assumptions illustrating the method, not measured benchmarks.
Deep discounting can damage brand — the source explicitly says it is not advocating discounting 'like crazy'.
The result is highly sensitive to whether the assumed conversion lift from discounting actually materializes; if it does not, the deeper-discount scenario loses money.

cards.title: Price prepaid bundles by comparing margin loss against retention gain
cards.summary: Prepaid multi-order bundles cut per-order margin but lock in multiple orders, so evaluate them on total lifetime profit rather than the discounted order's gross profit alone.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch or expand 3/6/12-order prepaid bundles, subscribe-and-save tiers, or any offer that trades discount depth for committed repeat orders.
steps: Model three segments side by side: one-time buyers, a three-order prepaid, and a six-order prepaid. Source assumptions: $80 undiscounted AOV, $19 product COGS, $15 fulfillment, $34 total COGS, $46 gross profit and 58% gross margin for one-time buyers.

Apply the discount and record the margin hit: 25% off for three orders gives ~$60 collected vs $80, gross profit falls to $26; 30% off for six orders gives ~$56 collected, gross profit falls to $22 and margin to about 39%. The source notes gross profit is roughly cut in half at the six-order tier.
Expect most operators to conclude at this point that the discount is not viable. That is the moment to add the retention data rather than stopping.
Model retention on a cohort of 1,000 new customers over 12 months. One-time buyers: about 10% reach order 2, 5% reach order 3, 3% reach order 4 → 1.2 average orders per customer in year one.

Three-order prepaid: 100% retention for three consecutive months, then roughly 50% roll off and 50% re-enroll, repeating → about 5.6 average orders in 12 months. Six-order prepaid: 100% retention for six months, then ~50% churn/re-enroll → about 9 average orders.

Multiply lifetime orders by gross profit per order. One-time: 1.2 × $46 = ~$54 LTV. Three-order prepaid: 5.6 × $26 = ~$146 LTV (about +169%, +$92). Six-order prepaid: 9 × $22 = ~$198 LTV (about 4x, +$144 per enrolling customer).

Then model the mix effect, because only a fraction of customers will take prepaid. Source sandbox: shifting from 100% one-time to 85% one-time / 10% three-order / 5% six-order raises weighted-average LTV from $54 to $71, about +30% on the same customer base, flowing to gross profit and operating income.

Consider prepaid as a working-capital tool as well as an LTV tool: collecting cash upfront can let you finance the inventory you will ship to that customer with their own money (negative net working capital), which the source notes is common in B2B SaaS and education but rare in ecommerce.
caveats: The retention curves (10% to order 2, 50% prepaid roll-off and re-enroll) are described as realistic for the presenter's merchants, not guaranteed results.
LTV figures ignore the marketing cost to acquire those customers, so a prepaid tier with lower cash collected can produce lower LTV-to-CAC than a one-time buyer if acquisition cost is unchanged.
Prepaid cash is partly a liability: you owe fulfillment over future months, so spent prepaid cash is not free profit.

The source also notes increasing discounts over the customer lifetime (e.g. 10% first, 15% second, 20% third, 25% fourth+) as an alternative to flat subscribe-and-save, because flat incentives get customers who subscribe for the one-time offer and cancel.

cards.title: Build separate unit economics for transactional vs subscription customers
cards.summary: Transactional and subscription customers have different AOVs, discounts and cost structures, so model their unit economics on separate rows before forecasting any revenue.
cards.use_when: Building or rebuilding a subscription-box or subscribe-and-save financial model, or deciding whether subscription revenue is actually more profitable than your ad hoc channel.
steps: Build two unit-economics tabs or row sets: transactional (ad hoc, no loyalty program) and subscription. The source treats this as necessary because their retention behavior is very different and mixing them hides the truth.
For transactional: start from undiscounted AOV ($90 in the source), back out refunds (4% assumed) and discounts (5% assumed, e.g. email-capture offer), giving net AOV of about $81.99.

For subscription: undiscounted AOV is usually lower ($75 assumed) because subscribers buy smaller, more frequent orders, with 4% refunds and an average 20% subscribe-and-save discount, giving about $57 collected.

Break COGS into product cost and fulfillment separately and scale each to the AOV. Source transactional: about $7 product and $16.20 fulfillment; source subscription: about $6.50 product and $5.50 fulfillment on the smaller basket.
Add credit card processing at about 2.75% of collected revenue in both cases.
Resulting source figures: transactional contribution margin about $56, roughly 68%; subscription contribution margin about $33.40, roughly 59%. The subscription order is less profitable per order.

Do not stop at the per-order comparison. The source states subscription customers usually generate three to five times as much revenue per customer on a lifetime basis, which more than repays the lower per-order margin — hence the need to forecast retention separately before judging the channel.
caveats: 50–70% gross margin is described as typical for supplements specifically; do not carry that expectation to other categories.

The source simplifies to a single flat 20% subscribe-and-save for modeling purposes while noting that real high-retention programs use increasing discounts over the customer lifetime or prepaid bundles, which the source says can drive roughly 2.5x more lifetime spend than flat subscribe-and-save 20%.
All percentages are assumptions in a demonstration model, not measured results for a real brand.

cards.title: Forecast ad spend divided by CAC to drive new customer counts
cards.summary: In a subscription-box model, marketing spend is the master lever: ad spend divided by CAC yields new customers, and everything downstream flows from it.
cards.use_when: Building a 36-month growth forecast, sizing cash needs or runway, or testing how sensitive your plan is to CAC improvements.
steps: Lay out monthly ad spend as a ramp rather than a flat number. Source example: $5,000 in month 1, $10,000 month 2, then +$5,000 per month for six months, then +$10,000 per month for the next six, then +$15,000 per month through month 24, then +$25,000 per month, ending around $570,000 per month at month 36.
Divide ad spend by CAC to produce new customers acquired that month. This is the mechanism that converts a budget decision into customer counts and, via unit economics, into revenue and margin.

Set CAC assumptions by price point and channel mix rather than by ambition. Source starting point for a product around this price: $100 CAC initially, dropping to $75 through month 12 and $60 after that as brand awareness and organic grow.

Explicitly acknowledge that CAC is unknowable before launch — it depends on copy, product, brand awareness and audience — so treat these as placeholders to be replaced with your observed CAC after you go to market.
Note the wide legitimate spread: some brands at scale have CAC far below $100 due to heavy organic, while brands relying on paid to a very niche audience can be far above.

Use CAC break-even as the sanity check: if you lose money after CAC on every customer, scaling ad spend multiplies the loss rather than the business. Determine your per-order post-marketing contribution before increasing the ramp.

Revisit and re-tune ad spend, conversion and CAC at the end of the model build — the source describes this as the normal iteration loop, and it is also how you answer 'how much cash do we burn to reach a given revenue level'.
Separate the new-customer counts into transactional and subscription streams, since only a portion of acquired customers will be sold directly into subscription.
caveats: CAC of $100/$75/$60 are illustrative assumptions for one supplement business, not benchmarks.
The ad-spend ramp and 36-month horizon are a demonstration model; substitute your own capacity, funding and observed CAC path.
Acquisition cost is only one side — the model is invalid if the retention assumptions it feeds are not grounded in your own cohort data.

cards.title: Turn a contribution-margin model into a pricing and negotiation checklist
cards.summary: Because net margin per order is thin, identify each controllable line — freight, duties, pick and pack, packaging, 3PL, payment fees — and quantify what a dollar saved on each is worth at your order volume.
cards.use_when: Negotiating with a 3PL, carrier or supplier, evaluating a packaging change, or deciding where to spend optimization effort in an ecommerce P&L.
steps: Lay out the full net revenue to operating income waterfall per unit so every cost is visible on its own line: gross revenue, discounts, returns, shipping income, net revenue, product cost, import freight, duties and taxes, gross margin, pick and pack, packing materials, 3PL charges, shipping to customer, merchant fees, contribution margin, marketing, post-marketing contribution, opex, operating income.

Track each line period over period as both a dollar per order and a percent of net revenue. In the source case, product COGS moved from 29% to 27% of net revenue, pick and pack declined month over month (possibly from a better warehouse system), and fulfillment totaled $31 then $35 per order.

Watch the lines the source flags as volatile and worth close attention: import freight, duties and taxes, and shipping to customer — the presenter specifically notes freight costs varying wildly and shipping being a key management area for ecommerce.

Quantify the payoff of a fix: if you can negotiate or eliminate a couple of dollars from any individual expense, that becomes an extra few dollars per order, which across thousands of orders changes profit by tens of thousands.

Include payment processing explicitly. The source assumes about 2.75% of revenue for credit card processing in a subscription model and $3.65 to $3.79 per order in the case study — a line that scales with revenue and can be negotiated.

Compare margins across periods and treat per-unit visibility as the point: a standard P&L that lumps all product and fulfillment costs into one COGS bucket hides whether the unit economics are improving or deteriorating.
caveats: The case study's 29%/27% COGS, $31/$35 fulfillment and $3.65/$3.79 merchant fees are one brand's figures for two months, not benchmarks.

Fulfillment scope differs by product and location, so which charges fall into it will vary; the source recommends defining your own margin definitions and measuring them consistently rather than assuming an industry standard.
Saving a dollar only matters at volume — at low order counts the same per-order improvement is negligible.

cards.title: Define gross margin, contribution margin and post-marketing contribution consistently
cards.summary: Treat gross margin, contribution margin and post-marketing contribution as three distinct measures with different purposes, and use contribution margin as the base you optimize back from.
cards.use_when: Setting up your store's reporting definitions, briefing an analyst or account manager, or comparing your margins against others' quoted figures.
steps: Define gross margin as revenue minus product cost only — the profit made at the product level, and the highest of the three percentages. Example given: sell for $100, cost $20 to make and get to the warehouse, gross margin about $80.

Define contribution margin as revenue minus product cost minus fulfillment — everything needed to sell and deliver the product to the customer's door. The source treats this as the profit you have available to spend on marketing and other operating expenses, and the margin you work back from when optimizing the business.

Define post-marketing contribution as contribution margin minus marketing spend — the test of whether you actually made a profit after producing, delivering and acquiring the customer. The source calls this the lowest and a very important view of whether the business generates profit.

Keep the terms separate in your reports even though people use gross margin and contribution margin interchangeably; the source recommends defining them according to how you run your business and then measuring them as unique ideas.

Use contribution margin as the ceiling on what you can spend to acquire a customer. In the source case, $64 contribution margin means you have roughly $64 to spend before breaking even on the product.

Interpret the CAC ratio accordingly: contribution margin to CAC of about 1.5 on the first order in the source example meant profitable on the first order, so all subsequent orders were effectively pure profit because they carry little or no marketing.
caveats: The source notes these terms are commonly used interchangeably in the industry, so when comparing to external figures, verify which definition the other party is using.
Contribution margin excluding marketing can look healthy while post-marketing contribution is negative, which is why the source insists both be tracked.
